Part I. Installation and configuration

1. System requirements

Item Minimum Recommended
Operating system Windows 10 / Ubuntu 20.04 / macOS 12 any 64-bit, current
Python 3.10 3.11
RAM 4 GB 8 GB
Free disk space 3 GB 5 GB
CPU 2 cores 4 cores or more
GPU not required not required (CPU inference is sufficient)
Browser any with WebSocket support Chrome / Firefox / Edge, current

Training the model from scratch takes about five minutes on four CPU cores; no GPU is needed at any stage.

2. Installation

2.1 Obtain the sources

Clone the repository from GitHub (or unpack the delivered archive):

git clone https://github.com/EDXiaoM/MaritimeRouteAI.git
cd MaritimeRouteAI

On Windows without Git, use Code → Download ZIP on the GitHub page, unpack the archive and open a command prompt in the unpacked folder.

2.2 Create an isolated environment

python -m venv .venv
source .venv/bin/activate        # Linux / macOS
.venv\Scripts\activate           # Windows

2.3 Install the dependencies

python -m pip install --upgrade pip
pip install -r requirements.txt

If pip cannot reach the default PyTorch wheels, install the CPU build explicitly:

pip install torch --index-url https://download.pytorch.org/whl/cpu

2.4 Verify the installation

pip install -r requirements-dev.txt
pytest

All tests must pass. Tests that need the trained model are skipped automatically when models/zone_classifier.pt is absent.

3. Preparing the data and the model

The archive already contains a trained model (models/), so this section is needed only to retrain or to use a different corpus.

The labelled corpus is attached to the GitHub release v1.0 as merged_geojson_v2.zip (https://github.com/EDXiaoM/MaritimeRouteAI/releases/download/v1.0/merged_geojson_v2.zip); unpack it into data/raw/.

# 1. put the labelled corpus here:
#    data/raw/merged.geojson
python scripts/prepare_dataset.py            # ~16 s, cleaning + features, writes data/processed/
python scripts/train_model.py                # ~5 min on CPU, writes models/
python scripts/evaluate_regions.py           # optional: accuracy per sea region
python scripts/benchmark_routing.py          # optional: 6 European voyages, all methods
python scripts/regional_examples.py          # optional: 11 regional voyages + map figure
python scripts/make_figures.py               # optional: regenerate the figures

prepare_dataset.py removes the points whose class contradicts their measured height or depth. Both measurements of a point, noaa_depth and elevation, are checked; at the default tolerance of 5 m (LABEL_CHECK_TOLERANCE_M in config.py) 5 427 of the 156 838 points are removed and 151 411 remain. Pass --no-clean to keep them.

prepare_dataset.py writes:

File Content
data/processed/zone_dataset.npz feature matrices and labels for the three splits
data/processed/dataset_statistics.json corpus statistics, cleaning report and per-region counts
models/reference_index.npz label-free bathymetry / OSM index

train_model.py writes:

File Content
models/zone_classifier.pt network weights and architecture
models/feature_scaler.joblib fitted standardiser
models/model_metadata.json hyper-parameters, metrics and training history

4. Running the application

python scripts/run_server.py

Then open http://127.0.0.1:8000.

Options:

python scripts/run_server.py --host 0.0.0.0 --port 8080
python scripts/run_server.py --reload          # development: auto-reload

5. Configuration

All tunable values live in src/maritime_route/config.py. The most useful ones:

Setting Default Meaning
ZONE_COST 1.0 / 1.8 / ∞ / ∞ traversal weight of each zone
ROUTING.grid_resolution_deg 0.25 default lattice step, degrees
ROUTING.max_grid_cells 400 000 lattice budget; larger areas are coarsened
ROUTING.safety_margin_cells 1 width of the penalised belt along the shore
ROUTING.proximity_penalty 1.6 extra cost of a water cell next to land
GENETIC.* see file default population size, generations, rates and seed of the genetic algorithm
routing/parameters.py see file since version 1.3 every parameter of the lattice and of the four methods is set in the interface (panel Algorithm parameters); this file defines their defaults, ranges and help texts
LABEL_CHECK_TOLERANCE_M 5.0 tolerance of the data-cleaning check, metres
REGIONS eleven boxes the sea regions used for per-region evaluation
TRAINING.* see file network size, epochs, learning rate, seed
SERVER.progress_interval_s 0.15 minimum interval between progress frames

Several settings can also be overridden with environment variables, which is convenient for deployment:

export MR_HOST=0.0.0.0
export MR_PORT=8080
export MR_DB_PATH=/var/lib/maritime/routes.db
export MR_MODEL_DIR=/opt/maritime/models
export MR_OUTPUT_DIR=/var/lib/maritime/exports
export MR_RESULTS_DIR=/var/lib/maritime/results   # JSON result files (default outputs/results)

6. The database

SQLite is created automatically at data/maritime_route.db on first start; the schema is in src/maritime_route/storage/schema.sql. No database server has to be installed. To reset the stored history, stop the application and delete the data/maritime_route.db* files.

7. Offline operation

The client requests OpenStreetMap tiles when the machine is online. If the tile service is unreachable, after four failed tiles the client switches by itself to the on-board chart — tiles rendered by the server from the model's own classification — and the application stays fully usable. The layer can also be selected manually in the layer control at the top-left corner of the map.

8. Troubleshooting

Symptom Cause and remedy
503 Model weights not found the model has not been trained — run scripts/train_model.py
The status pill shows reconnecting… the server was restarted; the client reconnects by itself with exponential back-off
Address already in use another process holds port 8000 — start with --port 8081
Planning reports no navigable path departure or destination is landlocked; the lattice is already refined and widened three times automatically
Planning reports lies on land the port is more than 60 km from any navigable cell, often because it lies outside the eleven sea regions covered by the training data
The genetic algorithm reports no navigable route evolved the evolutionary search converged on a closed strait; use A*
A red banner The route crosses land … the automatic coastline check could not correct the route (the neural network takes too much land for water there); set the grid resolution to 0.1° and build again, or check the passage on an official chart
No coastline-check banner appears the package global-land-mask is not installed — pip install -r requirements.txt
Step limit reached before the goal the maximum number of steps of the method is too small for this course; raise it in Algorithm parameters (for example ×100) or use A* instead of Dijkstra
The search takes too long press ■ Stop, or set a Time limit; use a coarser lattice, via points, or the heuristic weight of A* above 1
Where are the result files? outputs/results of the project (or MR_RESULTS_DIR); the path is shown after every search and on the Data tab
The map is blank no internet access — switch to On-board chart (offline) in the layer control
ModuleNotFoundError: maritime_route run the scripts from the project root, or set PYTHONPATH=src

Part II. Working with the application

1. Starting the application

Run python scripts/run_server.py and open http://127.0.0.1:8000.

The header shows two indicators:

  • live connection — the real-time channel to the server is open. While it reads reconnecting… the application still works through ordinary HTTP requests, only without live progress.
  • model 96.9% acc — the loaded classifier and its test-set accuracy.

The window is split into the control panel (left) and the chart (right). The panel has five tabs: Plan, Data, Compare, Model, History.

Interface language. The buttons EN / RU / 中文 at the right of the header switch the interface between English, Russian and Chinese at any moment, also after a search: the results on the screen are redrawn in the new language. The first time, the language of the browser is used (English if it is none of the three); the choice is then remembered in the browser. Result files, PDF reports and exports are always in English, so they read the same for everybody. (Интерфейс на русском языке — кнопка RU; 中文界面 —— 按 中文。)

2. Planning a route

2.1 Setting your own route: departure, destination, via points

Any route can be set; the presets are only examples. Three equivalent ways:

  • Click the chart. The first click sets the departure (marker A), the second the destination (marker B). The hint above the coordinate fields says which one the next click will set; the buttons Set A on chart and Set B on chart choose it explicitly, Swap A ⇄ B exchanges them.
  • Drag the markers. Both markers can be dragged; the coordinate fields follow.
  • Type the coordinates into the four fields, or press one of the preset chips (Kiel → Tallinn, Rotterdam → Lisbon, Helsinki → Copenhagen, Odesa → Novorossiysk, Piraeus → Thessaloniki, and the complex courses Gdańsk → Bergen, Jeddah → Dubai, Piraeus → Rhodes, Singapore → Hong Kong, Rotterdam → Gdańsk). The Piraeus presets also set the grid resolution to 0.1°, which the island-dense Aegean Sea needs; the other presets restore the default of 0.25°.

Via points (version 1.3). A complex course — round a peninsula, through a chosen strait, past a chosen side of an island group — can be forced through intermediate points: Shift + click on the chart (or press Add via point and click as many times as needed, then press it again) adds a yellow numbered marker. The route then passes through the points in their order; every leg is planned on its own lattice. Via points can be dragged, removed with a right click or with the × in the list under the coordinates, or all at once with Remove all.

2.2 Choosing the parameters

Control Meaning
Search algorithm A* — heuristic search, the default; Dijkstra — uniform cost, same result, more nodes; Genetic algorithm — evolutionary search: a population of candidate routes is improved by selection, crossover and mutation under a fitness function; it gives no guarantee of optimality and is shown for comparison; Dynamic programming — solves the Bellman equation for the cost to the destination of every cell (value iteration) and follows it from the departure; exact, same result as A*; Great circle — the naive shortest-distance reference
Grid resolution lattice step in degrees (0.02–1°). Finer resolution follows narrow straits more precisely but costs more time.
Algorithm parameters a panel with the parameters of the lattice and of the selected method (see below)
Service speed used only to convert the route length into a passage time
Show zone classification layer overlays the classified cells on the chart
Live zone read-out classifies the point under the pointer continuously and shows the zone, confidence and depth at the bottom-left of the chart

Algorithm parameters (version 1.3). Every method has its own parameters, and they are set in the application, not in the code. Open the panel Algorithm parameters under the grid resolution: it shows the group Lattice and run and the group of the method selected above. Hover over a label for its explanation and default. A changed value is shown in amber and counted in the panel title; Reset to defaults restores the shown groups. The values are remembered in this browser.

Group Parameter Default Meaning
Lattice and run Lattice cell budget 400 000 largest lattice classified; a larger box is coarsened
Margin around the points 2° space around the rectangle of the points
Diagonal moves on 8 or 4 neighbours of a cell
Near-shore band / penalty 1 cell / 1.6 extra cost of water next to land
Automatic lattice refinement / maximum refinements on / 3 finer lattice when no route exists
Coastline check on check against the 1 km land mask and correct (2.5)
Land mask in the correction / from the first lattice on / off block cells that the mask shows as land
Land share that blocks a cell 0.75 share of land samples in a cell that blocks it
Adaptive search area on widen the area when the passage lies outside it
Two-level search (corridor) / half-width on / 50 km fine lattice only around the coarse route
Time limit 0 = none the search stops after this time
A* Maximum number of steps 1 000 000 cells taken from the queue; 0 = no limit
Heuristic weight 1 above 1: weighted A*, faster, at most that factor above the optimum
Dijkstra Maximum number of steps 1 000 000 as for A*; Dijkstra needs several times more
Dynamic programming Maximum number of sweeps 0 = until convergence Bellman-equation sweeps
Genetic algorithm Population size, Generations (epochs), Early stop after 80, 300, 60 size and length of the evolution
Tournament size, Crossover and Mutation probability, Elite 3, 0.9, 0.35, 2 operators
Maximum waypoints, Land penalty, Random seed 14, 200, 42 chromosome length, fitness weight of land, reproducibility

2.3 Building the route

Press Build route. A progress block reports each stage:

  1. Building geographic lattice
  2. Neural network classifying grid cells — with the number of cells done
  3. Cost map ready — with the share of each zone
  4. A* search in progress — with nodes expanded and frontier size (for Dijkstra the same; for the genetic algorithm Genetic algorithm: evolving routes with the generation number and the best route cost so far; for dynamic programming Dynamic programming: solving the Bellman equation with the sweep number and the number of values improved in it)
  5. Coastline check: correcting the route — only when the first route crosses land on the independent coastline (see 2.5)
  6. Route ready

Timer and Stop (version 1.3). The progress block shows a timer and the time limit, if one is set. ■ Stop ends the search at once — within a fraction of a second, at any stage (classification, search, correction). A search that reaches a limit ends by itself. In every case the outcome is shown and saved to a file:

Outcome Meaning and what to do
Route found the route is drawn
Step limit reached before the goal the method made its maximum number of steps (A*, Dijkstra), sweeps (dynamic programming) or generations (genetic algorithm); raise it in the parameters — for example from 1 000 to 100 000 — and build again
Time limit reached raise the time limit or use a coarser lattice
Stopped by the user the Stop button was pressed
No navigable route between the points the finest lattice tried has no passage; try via points, a finer lattice or a larger margin

If no route is found — because a strait is narrower than one lattice cell, or because the only passage lies outside the rectangle around the two ports — the message Adapting the lattice appears: when the water around both points reaches the edge of the lattice, the search area is widened (the passage lies outside it); otherwise the lattice is refined (up to three times). A departure or destination is moved onto the nearest navigable cell only if that cell is within 60 km; a point further inland is reported as lying on land.

The genetic algorithm may fail to find a navigable route where A* succeeds (it can converge on a strait that the lattice closes). In that case the lattice is not refined, because A* has proved that a route exists; choose A* instead.

2.4 Reading the result

The chart shows:

  • the optimised route, coloured per zone along its length;
  • the great-circle route as a red dashed line;
  • the zone classification layer, if enabled.

The Route summary panel reports the route length, the great-circle distance, the detour ratio, the weighted traversal cost, the estimated passage time, the planning time, the number of expanded nodes and the number of waypoints. Below it, the Zone profile bar shows how much of the route lies in each zone.

How the route was found (version 1.3) opens a table of every lattice the planner tried: cell size, number of cells, steps, seconds and outcome, and what it did next (finer lattice, wider area, corridor ⟂ of the two-level search, next leg of a route with via points).

Result file (version 1.3). Above the summary a green box shows where the result was saved: the absolute path of a JSON file, a Copy path button and Download JSON (see 2.6).

2.5 Coastline check

Every route is checked automatically against an independent coastline — the 1 km GLOBE land mask of the package global-land-mask, which plays no part in the classification. The route is sampled every kilometre; the first and the last 5 km (the quays) are not checked. A banner above the route summary shows the outcome:

Banner Meaning
green — Coastline check passed no land on the route, or it only touches the coast for less than 3 km
amber — the first route crossed land … and was corrected automatically the neural network had taken some land for water; the cells under that land were blocked and the route searched again (if necessary on a finer lattice); the route shown passes the check
red — ⚠ The route crosses land … the automatic correction could not remove the land; the places are marked on the chart with red circles. Do not follow such a course; try a finer grid resolution or check the passage on an official chart

A port given by a city-centre coordinate lies on land, and the straight connector from it to the open water may cross the shore: such land touching the quay is counted as the port approach and is not an error. The result of the check is also written to the PDF report (line Coastline check), to the GeoJSON export and to the database.

The check needs the package global-land-mask (installed with requirements.txt); without it the banner is not shown and the application works as before.

2.6 Result files

Every search — found, not found, step limit, time limit or stopped — and every comparison of the methods is saved as a JSON file in the folder outputs/results of the project (another folder can be set with the environment variable MR_RESULTS_DIR). The folder is shown on the Data tab with the latest files. The name tells the points, the method, the outcome and the search time without opening the file:

route_N54.3233E10.1228_N59.4370E24.7536_dijkstra_step_limit_5.44s_20261014-134803.json
route_N54.3233E10.1228_N59.4370E24.7536_via1_astar_found_3.72s_20261014-134827.json
compare_N54.3233E10.1228_N59.4370E24.7536_5-methods_7.93s_20261014-134822.json

The file holds the request (points, method, resolution, speed), all parameters used, the status and its text, the timing (search seconds, start and end time), the search (steps, step limit, lattices tried), the route (length, cost, zones, coastline check) and all points with latitude, longitude, zone, cumulative distance and course. JSON keeps this structure in one file that Python (json.load), Excel (Power Query), MATLAB (jsondecode) or any GIS reads without a special parser. Example in Python:

from maritime_route.export.results import load_result
doc, points = load_result("outputs/results/route_...json")
print(doc["status"], doc["timing"]["search_seconds"], len(points))

3. Comparing with the shortest route

The Compare tab is filled automatically after every route. It reports the length of both routes, the additional distance accepted by the optimised route, how many sample points of the great circle fall on land, and a verdict: a great-circle route that crosses land is not navigable at all, so the extra distance is the price of a route that can actually be sailed.

Press Compare algorithms to run A*, Dijkstra, dynamic programming, the genetic algorithm and the great circle on one shared cost map of the same course, with the parameters set on the Plan tab (the time limit applies to each method separately; the timer and Stop work as for one route). The routes of all methods are drawn on the chart in the colours of the table. The first table reports for each method the outcome, route length, cost, how far above the optimum it lies, the steps made (for dynamic programming the Bellman updates, for the genetic algorithm the routes evaluated), the step limit and the search time. The second table puts the measured work next to the theoretical complexity — O((V + E) log V) for A* and Dijkstra, O(S · E) for dynamic programming, O(G · P · L) for the genetic algorithm — and its worst-case bound for this lattice. Then follow the node reduction of A* against Dijkstra, the cost differences and the size of the lattice. The reported times exclude the shared cost-map construction, so they compare the search methods only. The comparison is saved to a compare_….json file.

4. Working with AIS data

Open the Data tab and drop a .geojson, .csv or .json file onto the drop zone (or click it to browse).

  • CSV files must contain latitude and longitude columns; the usual spellings (lat, lon, lng, y, x, …) are recognised automatically.
  • GeoJSON files must be a FeatureCollection of points.

The application validates the file, classifies the points and stores them in the database. The report shows how many features were read, how many were valid, how many were dropped and how the points are distributed over the four zones. If the file carries class_code labels, the agreement between the model and those labels is reported as well.

The classified points are drawn on the chart and can be downloaded as Points GeoJSON or Points CSV.

The Database block at the bottom of the tab shows how many sessions, points, routes and waypoints are stored and how large the database file is.

5. Exporting the results

After a route has been built, three buttons appear under the route summary:

Button File Content
GeoJSON route_<id>.geojson route line, every waypoint with its zone, and the great-circle reference line
CSV route_<id>.csv waypoint table: sequence, coordinates, zone, weight, cumulative distance, bearing
PDF report route_<id>.pdf voyage summary (including the coastline check and its warning, if any), zone profile, comparison with the shortest route, model information and the waypoint list

The GeoJSON file carries styling properties (stroke, marker-color) and opens directly in QGIS, geojson.io and similar tools.

6. Inspecting the model

The Model tab reports the architecture, the number of input features and parameters, the size of the reference index, and the full test-set metrics: accuracy, macro and weighted F1, Cohen's κ and macro ROC-AUC. Below them the confusion matrix is shown cell by cell, together with the training and validation curves of the run that produced the deployed weights.

7. Stored routes

The History tab lists the routes saved in the database, newest first, with the algorithm, length, creation time, number of waypoints, search time and detour ratio. Clicking an entry draws that route on the chart again.
